# Capabilities

**Generated by `tools/capabilities.py generate`; do not edit.** The input
is `docs/capabilities.toml`, the only file a person edits. `docs/SCOPE.md`
defines what belongs in the kernel; this file records where it stands.

One capability per thing a caller would ask for, not per type and not
per module. Each verdict cites the symbols and tests that back it, and
`tools/check.sh` fails if they drift apart.

## Where the kernel stands

| `partial` | 8 |

### ogeom-bool

- **bool.booleans**: The boolean operations: cut, fuse, common, section and split, exact and fuzzy, with argument checking · `covered`
- **bool.cells**: The cells builder: arbitrary take/remove over the fused arrangement · `covered`
- **bool.defeaturing**: Removing a set of faces from a solid by extending and re-intersecting its neighbours · `partial`
  - *restriction:* Inner-loop features (bores, bosses, pockets whose rim is a
surviving face's inner wire) remove in full generality: wire surgery, no
re-intersection, the block back to the last bit. Band features (fillets and
chamfers along an edge) close for any number of bands in one call, each
running straight through with two end faces or wrapping with none, and
bands meeting at a corner close together: each recovers its own crease,
the corner is where one crease pierces the other's side, and a wedge's
flush cap named with its band folds into the band's crease; a tangent
chain's bands close together too (a stadium's rim rounded in one call),
the junction being the foot on either crease of the cross-section edge the
two bands share, and a band across a circular crease's seam read as one
run about its own centre rather than its complement; a rebuilt
face whose surface has no closed-form pcurves fits them by projection,
tolerances widened by the measured offset. A rim blend (a drum's top, a
bore's mouth, a boss's seat) takes a whole ring out of its neighbours and
closes on the circle they meet along: the neighbours' surfaces tell that
wound from a bore's, whose faces never meet and whose rings are simply
dropped, and a neighbour's own outer boundary may be the ring, so a drum's
cap grows back to its rim. The wall's seam reaches the recovered circle,
which is where it is cut and what the seam extends to meet. Wires are
spliced in the face's own order, since a seam stands in its wire twice,
and a gap that leaves and arrives at one vertex is wound the way the rim
it replaces was. A feature of several faces each bordering only one of
the neighbours that must meet again (a step along an edge, a notch cut
from a corner, a pocket open at an edge) closes by extension: every two
neighbours whose surfaces meet across the wound close the stretch of that
curve it took, as a new edge between the faces it pierces where they share
none there, or by running on an edge they share, cut short or split, to
where a third neighbour pierces the curve or to the other half's end.
Neighbours the wound left on one surface facing one way (a slot right
across a top, its two halves on one plane) come back as one face through
both halves' surviving edges, and a curve two neighbours meet along that
no other face stops (a rebate round a drum's rim) is taken whole, closing
on itself at the wall's seam: the box and the drum come back exactly. What
stays refused by name: a wound whose sides meet in no curve and lie on no
one surface, a removal that would leave a face with no boundary and no
edge to grow to, and a gap the recovered edges do not bridge.
- **bool.glue**: Gluing shapes along known-coincident boundaries · `divergent`
  - *reasoning:* Subsumed, and recorded as a settled decision in docs/PLAN.md: the boolean's same-domain unification already skips nothing it needs and unifies what glue would, so a separate glue mode would be a second spelling of the fuse with a faster wrong answer available. MakeConnected's job (conformal multi-body assembly) falls out of the fuse plus history.
- **bool.make-periodic**: Making a shape periodic so instances tile without seam duplication · `covered`
- **bool.make-volume**: Making volumes from a soup of faces: the arrangement's closed cells · `covered`

### ogeom-fillet

- **fillet.bitangent**: Bi-tangent blend construction · `divergent`
  - *reasoning:* Subsumed, per the settled decision in docs/PLAN.md: the 2D repertoire carries bi-tangency in the plane and the blend family's own envelope carries it in space, so a separate bi-tangent constructor would be a third spelling of two existing ones.
- **fillet.chamfers**: Chamfering edges: symmetric, two-distance, distance-and-angle · `covered`
- **fillet.corners-2d**: Filleting and chamfering the corners of planar wires · `covered`
- **fillet.edge-blends**: Blending edges: constant and variable radius fillets, rolling-ball, marched where no closed form exists · `partial`
  - *restriction:* Single edges, tangent chains and full rims blend, constant and variable radius, and the corner where three blends meet is closed: a rim where a flat cap meets a coaxial cylinder or cone (a drum's top, a frustum's foot, a tapered bore) rounds to its exact torus band, where the tube stands clear of its axis, and to the fitted band where that is what builds. a corner blend applied through the boolean's tangency at a face's own vertex. The marched fillet carries the rolling ball to topology on seats no closed form speaks (a fitted seam between two analytic walls, a conic seat re-opened to its full loop), with the blend fitted through the ball's own arcs and the legs melting on the hosts' exact surfaces. An open seat runs out: where the crease ends at a wall the band runs on until the ball has left the solid and the cut trims it against the wall, a straight band so across a boss's cylinder or cone cutting its corner away obliquely (a D-shaped block's chord, its wall square, drafted or overhanging, its drum upright or drafted) where it runs out alone; where the faces at its end all turn back behind the crease (a re-entrant turn of its wall, however slight), its continuation runs into the material and the band stops at the vertex; where it ends at a split (a seam vertex, or a neighbouring blend's own rail), the band is capped in the end section's own plane, and two such blends meet cap to cap along the shared arc, both caps consumed, in either order. Two convex creases of one request that share a face and turn at a vertex meet there: carried on past it each is a straight band of its end section, and two of one radius cross in the plane bisecting their centre lines, exactly where the reflection in it carries one end section onto the other (a flat shared host, walls whose tangent planes at the vertex reflect into each other). There, across a re-entrant turn both run on to that plane and take the corner cell both hold, where the material holds it (a straight band between planes whose end section reaches past that plane, its wall drafted out under the corner as a moulded pocket's are, is carried on past it and cut back to it); across a convex turn of a curved crease both stop in it where the bands' curvature keeps their sections there within a marched band's fit; either way the two are joined across it into one wedge. Where the end sections differ and both creases are straight (a drafted wall beside a square one), across a re-entrant turn each band is carried on with what stands past its wall and the two are intersected in one boolean, so the corner takes what lies above both bands, bounded by their own intersection, where the material holds it all. Across a convex turn of two straight creases, whatever their sections (an acute, square or obtuse outside corner, its walls square or leaning alike or apart), each band runs out as it does alone and the cuts take their union, as they do where one of the two is a drum's rim beside a straight crease (a D-shaped block's arc beside its chord, in either order, its drum upright or drafted) and, past where they meet flush, beside a spline crease (a rib's wall running into a boss's rim, the rib's band run out past the vertex as alone). Across a re-entrant turn one of the two may be a drum's rim beside a straight crease, the material within the drum (a boss fused onto a block whose wall leans either way, the boss upright or overhanging, a cone narrowing to its foot or standing out at it) or outside it (a bore up to a drafted chord): the rim's torus band is taken from its cap to where its section stands wholly past the other wall, widened by what stands off the drum before the rim's cap (beside the chord's own band too, where a chord through the bore's axis or past it leans off the drum), intersected so, less what stands off the drum past the other wall, and the rest joined back on. A bore whose chord wall overhangs meets as without a junction, where the band carried on past the rim's cap would reach under the pocket's floor, and so does a cone standing out at its foot beside a square wall close to the rim's cap, where that band crosses the cone at a turn the boolean reads as a touch. A loop of junctions closes, its last junction taken and the ring's wedge sewn to itself (a square pocket's rim meets at all four corners, and a disc's pocket up to a chord at both). Crossed junctions stand beside flush ones in a loop or chain of the request's edges, the flush ones taken first; a band crossed at both ends is cut in two halfway along, each half joined into its own corner and the two joined again where both hold the band's one section. Inside corners off square in plan and corners whose walls both lean are taken, the open corner past both walls' planes taken out of the two widenings, and so is every corner of a pocket off square in plan whose walls each lean their own way. Elsewhere (a crossed junction that would leave two joined bands meeting without one, a turn folding back past the solid, a wider convex turn of two curved bands, or of a curved band other than a drum's rim beside one of another kind) the later seat runs on through the earlier band or the caps stand, as without a junction, and so wherever the meeting does not close. An L-bracket's end rim blends over its re-entrant band as one tangent chain (line, the band's own end arc, line), the ball rolling on the concave cylinder between the lines, to the closed form. A fill and a wedge asked together stop at each other, since only blends that round the same way run on through one another's bands; whichever is asked first takes the corner, and both orders are exact. Cone, sphere and torus hosts march and blend: the chart inverted in closed form, a band's connector fitted where no closed form lifts the chart segment, a looping seat with a corner at its join steered by a smooth refit of itself, the band's first station re-solved on the apex column so a rim opened at the host's own seam leaves no sliver; a full circular rim whose hosts are not a cap and its coaxial wall takes the march too. A fitted host marches: its chart inverts by projection, a closed patch's seam wraps as a period does, the patch is continued past the face by a few radii so the ball can run out, a seat the boolean split into arcs is closed back through the neighbours the hosts share and marched as the loop it is, the rail loop slid into the host's own window, and the wedge melts: a straight edge of a converted box, the crease round a converted post split at its seam, a converted cone's rim, a converted drum's rim. Under it a marched section the centripetal fit misses is fitted again by chord length, and a loop cut at a closed patch's seam is closed on it; a melt the boolean still cannot resolve refuses by name. A rim beside a sphere's pole whose rail passes over the pole blends with the sphere's leg running from the rail to the pole, the rim cut from it. A bore whose wall toward the pole is thinner than the ball blends the same way. A rail passing the pole closer than one stride of the march, where its chart turns half round faster than the stations follow, is taken on the same sphere charted with its pole on another axis of its frame and its seam through the widest gap between the seat and the faces' edges: the leg is built there and the solid's faces on the sphere are rebuilt on that chart, their old seam and pole edges dropped. Where those faces are not the sphere less some disks (or one disk less others) on the turned chart, the rail is refused by name. A seat whose hosts turn tangent at an end of the crease (the seam of two equal drums crossing, at the points where they touch) pinches there: the stations are solved one by one toward the pole, the pole's collapsed section closes the band, and the wedge has no cap at that end. A tangency inside a crease with none at its ends is refused by name. A straight crease whose faces are planes or drums parallel to it (a wall meeting a drum along a ruling) blends exactly: the section swept straight, its band a drum of the fillet's radius. A vertex where a curved face meets rounds with the one ball touching its three surfaces, its centre walked to a radius in from each and its compartment bounded by the planes through the centre and each pair of touch points, so each band's end section is the ball's own; `fillet_edges` closes such a corner, and the bands one at a time with the corner tool after agree with it to rounding when the ruling's band goes first, or when the rim arc's band goes first: the straight band's section through the rim's torus runs tangent to the torus's end meridian into the corner, and ends at that vertex. The straight band first runs out across the drum past that vertex, as it does alone, and takes the corner with it; the ruling's band and the rim arc's after it agree in either order. The corner tool rounds any convex planar vertex. Where one ball touches every face (a square or oblique trihedral corner, a square pyramid's four-edged apex), its block is the polyhedron of the N host planes and the N planes through the ball's centre square to the edges, where each band's rim and the ball's coincide. Where no single ball does (a rectangular pyramid's apex, an irregular pentagonal one), the region the ball's centre may occupy has a tip of several vertices joined by ridges, and the corner is the exact envelope of the rolling ball: a sphere at each tip vertex, cut with its own compartment, and the flush fillet of a virtual crease along each ridge, the compartments meeting cap to cap on the planes square to the ridges; a ridge seven microns long is kept as the sliver of cylinder it is. At more than three edges the corner goes first and the flush fillets follow, since bands built before the corner crash into each other at the apex. The ball's pole stands along a ridge where there is one, its seam turned from the corner, and otherwise the tool is offered on each of the corner's 2N labellings in turn, the first that closes standing; the boolean closes every labelling of an oblique corner and of a square pyramid's apex, one solid each time. The flush fillets follow at a sharp apex too, and after a corner whose sphere clears a fourth plane by a few hundredths of a millimetre, where the envelope keeps a sliver of that plane beside the patch and the band meeting the sliver runs a straight end tangent to the sphere's rim: a line and a circle share no stretch, so the tangency splits neither. The curved-seat corner is closed in either order: through `fillet_edges` a marched blend and a straight one meet at their corners, the later's run-out walking on under the earlier band, and the boolean decides once per shared edge piece whether it is dust. A sub-piece of one edge lies in several charts, each with its own snap, so deciding once means a sliver that one chart collapses is collapsed in every chart. Where three or more edges of one `fillet_edges` call meet at a vertex, the corner tool closes it with the rolling ball's patch before the bands, which stop flush against it: a box corner's sphere octant, a pyramid apex's sphere or spheres and cylinders; a corner the tool does not speak keeps the bands' caps. `blend_faces` and `fillet_faces` round curved faces that share no edge: swept from one section where the surfaces share a direction or an axis, marched where they cross otherwise. Between separate faces a marched ball that touches both all the way round a closed seat (a tube through a floor at a slant, two pipes crossing) gives a band fitted closed round the loop, each face cut along its closed line of contact; a closed line across the seam of a closed B-spline face whose chart does not wrap round is refused by name, as the cut does not part the face. Refused by name too: faces the ball leaves at different places round its seat and never both at once, a line of contact crossing a face more than once, and a round crossing a face between the two (a ball wider than a chamfer between the faces it rounds). The ball touching both faces is the one the round's arc lies on, and a blend is refused by name where another face of the solid, on any surface, B-splines included, holds a point inside it at any station of the run (a chamfer, a round or a wedge between the faces, over all or part of the run), read over the whole run by halving between stations until the centre's travel fits under the face's clearance: the strip goes with the corner only where it lies wholly outside the ball. Between two planes and on the swept path only the ball's lune counts, the part of it between its centre and its arc, searched cell by cell over its section and the run where a face comes inside the ball: a part thinner than the ball, its far side reaching into the back of the ball only, is rounded, and an older, smaller round between the faces goes with the corner, the ball's side read inside the lune; the marched path asks the whole ball but reads the side inside the lune too, so an older round just smaller than its ball goes with the corner there as well. `blend_faces` and `fillet_faces` round every corner the surfaces cross in that the ball rolls in (a drum's flat and its wall, two drums fused), where the corners stand apart by more than their reach or a line parts the polygons holding their sections. Faces the crease or a line of contact meets, and faces holding a capped run's end, are where the round runs off and are not asked. Between two planes a blend is refused by name too where the ball touching both touches a face's plane off the face at a station of the run (a face narrower than the ball's setback). An edge round refuses by name where its faces meet tangent (no corner), where the ball's contact on a face stands past the face's far side in the material (a boss on the wall) or all along the edge (a face narrower than the setback, which a ball would roll over onto the face beyond), but for a convex straight edge beside a planar strip (a chamfer, a narrow top) whose far edge is convex too: where the strip lies wholly in the corner the ball touching the planes either side of it takes off, its ends on faces square to the edge, the round is that ball's and the strip goes with the corner. A concave straight edge beside such a strip whose far edge is straight and convex (the seam of two solids fused at a slant) rounds with the ball touching the other face and resting on that far edge, its centre on the ellipse, or the line, where the plane a radius off the face meets the cylinder a radius about the edge, the band fitted through the balls' arcs to the marched band's target with its rails on the face's plane and the edge's line, where over the whole crease the ball rests on that edge alone, its contact moving one way along it, touches the face within it, comes within its radius of no other face and its sections do not cross. Where the ball changes what it holds partway, the round is a chain of such bands meeting tangent on the section where the ball holds three things at once, each piece the ball's holding a face on each side (the cylinder between the planes), a face and an edge of the other face (the ellipse), or a face and a corner of the other face (the circle a radius over the face and a radius from the corner, its band's arcs all ending on the corner): it comes down on a strip that widens past its setback, narrows onto the other face's far edge, or rolls round a corner of a triangular strip onto its next edge, under the same conditions on every piece. It is refused by name where the ball comes onto the face beyond a far edge along the crease (it then rounds the corner between that face and the one it touches, another seam's round), rests on far edges of both faces at once, or leaves either face, and in a request where the edge shares a face or a vertex with another of its edges. It refuses also where it runs off a face anywhere along an edge of a request that shares a face or a vertex with another of its edges; an edge sharing neither runs off a face narrowing to a tip and is cut off there, as alone.

### ogeom-heal

- **heal.canonical-simplification**: Recognizing that exact geometry is secretly analytic: a B-spline that is a cylinder · `covered`
- **heal.custom-remodelling**: Rebuilding a shape's geometry wholesale: baking transforms, converting representations · `covered`
- **heal.fix-shape**: Fixing broken shapes: wires, faces, shells, solids, free bounds, small features · `partial`
  - *restriction:* `fix_shape` is the standalone entry point: diagnose, put a wire's edges end to end where an order exists, collapse edges shorter than their own vertices' tolerances, make one of two vertices a wire's edges meet at within the trim cap, fill a wider gap with a straight edge where it is provably the one lacking (shorter than every edge of each face it is in, no other vertex as near its ends, on each face's surface within the face's tolerance, each face checking clean after; any other gap stays reported), give a boundary crossing a pole its degenerate edge, fit missing pcurves, sew loose faces, strip a wire's tails (an edge out and one straight back along the same curve within their tolerances, on one copy of the chart, held by no other face; a hole of tails alone goes) and cut off its notches (an edge run back along part of the one before it, the longer cut where the shorter turns; check names two-edge tails and notches, not a slit of one edge), remove a hole held by no other face whose every point is within the face's tolerance of its boundary, on a plane, cylinder, cone, sphere, torus, B-spline patch, or revolution or extrusion of a B-spline (proved cell by cell on the chart drawn to a bound on the surface's first derivatives over the hole's box, closed form on the elementary surfaces and from the control net on a spline; the hole's area within the tolerance times its length is necessary, not sufficient; any other surface keeps its holes), mend a boundary crossing itself once in its chart (two consecutive edges crossing short of their vertex within the trim cap are cut back to the crossing and the vertex moved there; any other crossing of a one-wire face held by a container splits it into its two loops; each face changed checking clean after, anything else counted), bound a wireless face by its domain's sides (seam and pole edges) on a sphere, torus or patch, or mark it natural where those sides have no closed form (a wireless face on a plane, cylinder or extrusion stays reported: its domain is a working window, not an extent), state the gap between two free edges of a shell's or a compound's loose faces that are each other's only twin within the trim cap (the gap shorter than every edge of either face, no other vertex as near their ends) where sewing a copy shows it joins them, chain free edges into contours and wires (free_bounds), tighten tolerances, widen an edge to how far its pcurves stand off its curve and a vertex to how far its curves end from it (within the trim cap, as the readers record the same slop), orient each run of a shell's or solid's faces along their shared edges, turn a solid's run facing into its material as a whole, restore tolerance containment by widening what is bounded (`restore_containment`, which the STEP and IGES readers run on every body they build), diagnose again, and report what it did and what remains. Beneath it: reanchoring periodic rings, sewing, validity diagnosis, the reader's inline heal sequence, and the instructed fixes: fix_face_pcurves fits the trims the reader refused at a caller's cap, and reanchor_boundaries moves a boundary onto the surface it bounds with the displacement recorded in widened tolerances, both measured on community assemblies with boundaries millimetres off. fix_small_faces collapses a spot face to a point and a strip face to one long side, rebuilding its neighbours so the shell stays closed; remove_small_solids drops debris solids under a volume; solids_from_shells makes solids of closed shells, outer boundaries told from voids by which shell holds which vertex. self_union (in ogeom-bool, opt-in) resolves a solid whose boundary passes through itself into the union of the material it encloses: faces split where they cross, pieces kept where the winding number is zero beyond and positive behind; faces crossing one they share an edge or corner with, or folding through themselves, are refused. A STEP grid of patches reads as one spline surface. Healing here is measured by the imported corpus rather than claimed in general.
- **heal.same-parameter**: Diagnosing and repairing the same-parameter law between a curve and its pcurves · `covered`
- **heal.scripted-pipeline**: Resource-file-driven sequences of healing operators · `divergent`
  - *reasoning:* The job (run a heal sequence on import) exists and is done with a fixed inline sequence in the exchange readers, measured by the corpus. A pipeline scripted from resource files is configuration the applications that need it can build from the same functions; the kernel keeping a config-file interpreter would be an application affordance.
- **heal.status-reporting**: Statuses, messages and traversal support for the healing pipeline · `divergent`
  - *reasoning:* Healing outcomes here are values: `SameParameterReport`, `StepReport`, counts from `reduce_tolerances`. These are Rust Results rather than status bitfields read back through a registrator. A message-registration framework would add a second channel for what the return values already say.
- **heal.substitution**: Recording shape substitutions and applying them across a model · `covered`
- **heal.tolerances**: Reading and tightening the tolerances a shape actually needs · `covered`
- **heal.upgrade**: Upgrading shapes in place: same-domain unification, edge merging, subdivision, splitting along curves · `covered`

### ogeom-io

- **io.3mf-colours-and-roles**: 3MF colours from colour groups, base materials and textures, and the roles of objects and volumes · `partial`
  - *restriction:* Colour groups, base materials and texture groups read at
each triangle's corners, textures (PNG or JPEG parts) sampled by the
nearest texel and tiled as the texture says, `none` read as `clamp`.
Composite materials and multi-properties are passed over with a warning.
Roles (part, modifier, support blocker, support enforcer, negative volume,
or another as written) are read by name from objects' metadata and from
the configuration parts under `Metadata/`, by triangle range or by
component; a role kept in any other form is not seen, and the volume reads
as a part. A volume's triangles stay in its object's mesh, the volumes
saying which they are.
- **io.iges**: IGES, both directions: solids as manifold B-rep, sheets as trimmed surfaces, surface files sewn, units converted · `partial`
  - *restriction:* The core entity set reads and writes, and eight round-trip cases hold it to measured volumes: planes, a periodic
cylinder wall with its seam, a doubly periodic torus, a seam-only sphere, a
boolean result, a spline-walled prism through its tabulated cylinders
(122 over 126), a revolved spline profile through its surface of
revolution (120), and inch-unit scaling. The writer writes surfaces of
revolution, extrusions and offsets in their own spellings (120, 122, 140;
an offset as its analytic form where it has one, over a plane or spline
basis otherwise, any other offset as a spline patch), and the reader
reads each back as the same surface; a solid's whole name goes out and
comes back as its Name property (406 form 15). The reader also takes every axis-aligned conic arc (104: ellipse,
hyperbola, parabola, each as its own curve), ruled surfaces (118) as the
degree-one patch between the two curves' exact spline forms, and constant
offset curves and offset surfaces (130, 140). A conic whose axes turn is
read in the frame where its cross term vanishes and turned back, exactly;
parametric spline surfaces (114) convert exactly to bicubic B-splines; an
offset curve whose distance varies (linearly with arc length, or as a
function curve's coordinate) is fitted same-parameter with its base; and a
trim given only in a B-spline surface's parameters is lifted through the
surface. Model-space annotation (notes, leaders, labels, symbols and the
linear, radial, diametral, angular and ordinate dimensions) reads as PMI
callouts of the lines the file draws, a dimension whose text states a
number carrying that value as a semantic dimension. Subfigure instances
place their definition (308, 320) or base, built once and shared under each
placement: a singular instance (408) or a network instance (420) by its
scale, matrix and translation in the specification's order, a rectangular
(412) or circular (414) array at each position its DO or DON'T list keeps,
a group (402) as its base placing every member; a network instance
flagged logical (a schematic's), or scaling its axes unlike, is refused
by name, and connect points are not read; a definition's solids,
trimmed and untrimmed surfaces, constructive solids and curves are placed
with it; levels (with 406 level lists)
and groups (402) read as the document's layers. Constructive solids read
as the solids they describe: the block, wedge, cylinder, cone frustum,
sphere, torus and ellipsoid primitives (150 to 168), solids of revolution
and linear extrusion, boolean trees (180) through the kernel's own
booleans, solid assemblies (184) and solid instances (430). A trim given only
in the parameters of a plane, cylinder, cone, sphere or torus is lifted
through the format's parameterization, each surface framed by the reference
direction it names; on a tabulated cylinder (fractions of its directrix and
generator) and a surface of revolution whose generatrix is a line, a
spline, a circular arc or an ellipse with its axes along its plane's (the
generatrix's own parameter, an arc's or ellipse's its angle from the
format's start angle, and the angle turned). Independent
untrimmed surfaces (parametric spline, ruled, revolved, tabulated,
B-spline, and offsets of those) read as faces bounded by their own extent
and sew with the rest; the writer writes a face with no boundary as the
trimmed surface whose outer boundary is its surface's. Copious data drawn
as a path (106, forms 11 to 13 and 63) reads as the exact polyline through
its points, a trim taking each segment as an edge; a point set (forms 1
to 3) is no curve and is refused by name. Refused by name: a trim on a
surface of revolution of a hyperbola, parabola, turned ellipse,
composite, parametric-spline or offset generatrix, whose own IGES parameter this reader does not carry; a
drawing's own annotation stays on the sheet and is counted as skipped.
Independent curves that are geometry
(100, 102, 104, 106, 110, 112, 126, 130) read as wires, a composite
curve's matrix carrying its pieces and its points passed over, and the
writer writes a free wire or edge as an independent curve. Stand-alone
points (116) that are geometry read as vertices, and the writer writes a
free vertex as an independent point. A curve on a surface (142) builds its
trim from its model-space curve unless its preference flag prefers the
parameter-space curve, which is then lifted, the model-space curve
standing in where that lift fails. A parent's matrix carries the children
it owns physically, as IGES 5.3, section 3.2.3, table 4 lists them: a
trimmed surface's surface and boundaries, a subfigure definition's members,
a drafting entity's leaders and witness lines, a composite curve's pieces,
and the curves and surfaces the swept, ruled and offset entities are built
from; a child owned only logically stands where its own matrix puts it. An
independent bounded plane (108, form 1) reads as the face its curve
encloses. External references (416) to a definition or a whole file
resolve, through `read_iges_file`, against the files in the deck's own
directory, each file identified by the name its global section gives it
and a definition by the symbol its index (402, form 12) lists; a missing
file, a misnamed file, an unlisted symbol, a logical reference and a
reference to a natively kept definition are refused by name, as is every
reference in a deck read from text.

### ogeom-offset

- **offset.draft**: Drafting faces about a neutral plane for mould release · `partial`
  - *restriction:* Planar faces turn about their neutral line, walls of revolution (cylinders and cones) turn about their neutral circle into exact cones, and extruded walls (a spline profile swept straight) turn ruling by ruling about their neutral crossing's own tangent and re-fit, with the drafted angle held along the height. Every other face (a raw fitted patch, a wall of revolution about an oblique neutral) is drafted the way a mould-maker drafts: the ruled surface through the face's crossing with the neutral plane, rulings the pull turned by the angle, read off the face's own mesh and corrected onto the surface. A face the neutral plane does not reach turns about where its own surface, run on beyond the face, meets the plane: the planes' line, the neutral circle, the ruling's closed-form height, a drum's or cone's rulings run on to the plane, or a patch's crossing within its own extent; a patch that stops short of the plane has no extension to carry the hinge and is refused by name. A draft whose turned rulings cross inside the drafted window (a profile curled tighter than the draft's reach) is refused by name, as is a face the neutral plane crosses in two runs: a region beside both would turn about two hinges, and the face would split where the two turned supports meet, which a draft (the same faces on turned supports) does not do.
- **offset.filling**: Filling a boundary with a face: the plate surface · `covered`
- **offset.form-features**: The form features: prism, revolution, rib and slot against a base · `covered`
- **offset.loft**: Lofting through sections, ruled or smoothed · `partial`
  - *restriction:* The ruled loft takes two closed wire sections (coaxial parallel circles, or polygons of the same corner count whose ruled walls come out planar) or a section and a point: a cone on a circle's own axis, an exact pyramid over any straight loop. The skinned loft takes N closed sections, planar or not (a planar end is capped by its plane, a wavy end by a patch skinned from the rim to a point inside it), ends at a point on request, loops back on itself, and takes per-section alignment hints. A ruled wall between two segments that are not coplanar is the bilinear patch through its four corners, exact, so polygon sections may be turned against each other. `make_loft_solid` closes the loft sheet into a solid through N closed sections with planar ends, ruled or smooth: sections of different edge counts, lines, arcs and splines mixed, are split to match by arc length, every piece exact, so a ruled square to circle is exact; with guide curves the walls are the guided Gordon sheet, capped by the end sections' planes, holding every section exactly and every guide to ten confusions. Guided sections of several edges share one edge count and a guide runs through every corner where two edges meet; each edge's wall is the Gordon patch between the guides through its two corners. The skinned loft holds its sections exactly where they are exact: through two sections it is the ruled loft; through more with matching corners, one strip per edge meeting along seams through the corners, a plane wherever its rows share one; through coaxial circles, the revolution of a meridian through their radii.
- **offset.middle-path**: Extracting the middle path of a pipe-like solid · `covered`
- **offset.projection**: Projecting wires normally onto faces, pcurves riding along · `covered`
- **offset.shell-thicken**: Offsetting shapes and sheets, and thickening shells and sheets into solids · `covered`
- **offset.sweeps**: Sweeping profiles along spines: pipes, pipe shells, evolved shapes, the frame laws · `partial`
  - *restriction:* Pipes run a circular section along a spine edge, exactly for straight and circular spines and skinned for free-form and helical ones, and along a wire of lines and arcs, open or closed, as the pipe shell of the disc square to its start with its default mitres, wherever that sweeps it exactly: legs meeting tangent are the cylinders and torus segments they sweep, a closed one a ring with no cap, straight legs are mitred on the planes halving their corners, a sharp corner of a wire with arcs, between two lines or turning in the plane of the arcs beside it (a line and an arc, or two arcs), is the union of the legs and their straight run-ons outside the turn, each cut on the plane halving the corner in one half ellipse, the legs meeting inside the turn where each rim point's two paths cross, and a corner that turns an arc out of its plane, or turns in it so tightly that the paths inside it miss, is mitred in pieces. A wire the pipe shell refuses, or sweeps only as a skin (a free-form edge), is refused by name, as is a leg shorter than its corner's reach; the skinned pipe takes such a wire to a stated tolerance, as the pipe shell of its disc. `place_on_spine` brings a profile drawn elsewhere onto a spine's start before a sweep, rigidly about its centroid: turned square to the start tangent by the least rotation, moved so its centroid is the start point, or both. A pipe shell may bring its own profile on, as `PipeLaws::contact` asks: `PipeContact::Contact` moves it along its plane's normal until its plane runs through the start point (the start's foot on the plane is the contact point, so an open wire is moved as a face is), and `PipeContact::Correction` then turns it about the start by the least rotation standing it square to the start tangent; a profile with no plane, or whose plane holds the tangent, is refused by name. The evolved sweep runs a profile along a planar spine, exactly, by composition. The pipe shell sweeps an arbitrary planar profile, holes and all, along an open spine wire under a rotation-minimizing or Frenet frame law, and it also sweeps a profile round a closed spine, smooth or faceted, holes and all: the loop's holonomy paid off, a faceted profile skinned as one C1-closed strip per facet, each hole a void tunnel of its own shell. A sharp-cornered ring mitres exactly when its corners turn in the plane: the wrap is one more mitre, the seam must stand on a corner, and the planar Pappus volumes land to the last digit. The Frenet law rides the loop too (single-valued round it, so it owes no reconciliation), with every corner loop one rail shared by the two strips meeting there. A ring seamed mid-leg butts its two half-legs on the seam's own ring, and a skew-cornered ring closes on its mitres: the frame is reflected across each mitre plane, the loop's holonomy spread along the legs as a twist. A corner against a curved leg, on an open spine or a ring, ends both walls on the crossing of their generators, exact where the corner turns in the leg's plane. A skew corner against a curved leg keeps the reflected frame and mitres in pieces: each side is swept on straight past the corner, trimmed by the mitre plane, and the pieces fused, the difference between the two sections standing as a face of the mitre plane; a closed wire profile sweeps there as the walls of the face it bounds, the end caps taken off. Each spine edge skins its own run, so a spine whose curvature steps at a smooth join (an arc into its tangent line) is followed exactly, and a run whose sections share a plane is that plane. A spine of lines and arcs meeting tangent is swept exactly: each line leg an extrusion of the section, each arc leg its revolution about the arc's axis, the legs fused, so every wall is the plane, drum, cone, ball or torus its profile edge sweeps. Round sharp corners turning in the planes of the arcs beside them, with the default mitres, any planar face, holes and all (square tubing, a rectangle off the spine, a rounded slot), is swept exactly too: each edge's walls are those closed forms down each leg, outside a turn run on straight and cut on the plane halving the corner, where the two legs' run-ons are mirror images whatever the section's shape, and inside it cut on the curve where each point's two paths cross, a conic held exactly for a straight edge and a curve fitted within the stated tolerance for a curved one. Where the paths inside a turn miss, or an arc bends round an axis the section reaches, the general sweep takes the corner. `make_helical_sweep` is the screw motion of a profile in a plane through the axis, cylindrical or tapered, either hand: every point runs its own helix and the walls are fitted through those images in quarter turns. `make_pipe_shell_evolving` scales and twists the section linearly with the length run along the spine, and `make_pipe_shell_laws` by laws of its own: linear, the monotone cubic through given values, which keeps between neighbouring values (a scale through positive values stays positive), or a function of the share of the length run (`SpineFunction`), which gives the start value at the start and is read wherever a section is placed or the skin checked, a scale refused where it reads naught or below; a function law is never taken as standing still, so every run it moves along is skinned. Scaled linearly without a twist down one straight edge it is the ruled loft to the scaled image, exact (a pyramid's or cone's frustum, the pyramid or cone at a scale of zero); otherwise each loop is skinned through the placed sections and held to the tolerance against the law, along an open spine with no sharp corner, each hole a solid of its own cut from the outer. Round a smooth closed spine the section twists whole turns, unscaled, the skin closed on itself, or part of a turn where that brings each loop of the section home onto itself (a square a quarter turn, a circle about its centre any angle): a faceted loop's edges sweep strips open at both ends, each closing on the strip that lands where it began, a smooth loop is read from a point sliding round it as it turns; a scale, or a part turn the section's symmetry does not close, is refused there by name, as the section would not come home to itself; a twist law of any shape closes there where a linear one ending as it does would. Round sharp corners an evolving face sweeps run by run, mitred, extended or rounded: each run under the laws over its share of the length, from the section it starts with, the stretches where the laws stand still swept exactly; a twist still moving through a mitred corner turns the two legs' sections inside it against each other, so their skins cut the mitre plane along two curves that cross, and the mitre faces are the regions between them (see the glued mitres below); a skinned run into a curved leg's extended corner, its wall leaving the extension's side plane along its start edge as the scale narrows it, joins that extension however shallowly it leaves, so long as it rises past ten confusion distances by the first sample in. The multisection pipe takes faces with holes, as many in every section, each hole swept through the sections and cut from the outer solid. Round sharp corners a face is also swept run by run: the spine cut at its corners, each smooth run swept on its own (a straight run keeping its frame as the prism of the section), the runs mitred on the halving plane, extended or rounded, along open or closed spines and against curved legs. The auxiliary and binormal laws turn sharp corners this way too, their runs meeting a mitre with the sections the law sets; a straight run meeting a skinned one at a mitre takes the skin's own fit of each ring the two share within the tolerance (a hole or a smooth loop), so both cut the mitre plane alike; two skinned runs meeting at a mitre end on their sections exactly where a ring is one edge with an exact rational form (a circle, a conic, a B-spline), the later run starting on the earlier's end ring mirrored where the earlier is swept first, so both cut the mitre plane in one curve, and a holed section's ring that is a circle centred on the spine sweeps there as the exact tube every frame carries it along (a cylinder down a line, a torus round an arc), so a holed face mitres between two skinned runs; a section off the spine, solid or holed, mitres there too, the later run run back from its own skin's start rings. Where the fuse of two mitred runs cannot reconcile their cuts of the mitre plane (two fits of one curve where the frames mirror across it, as round a symmetric lens, or curves that cross at a shallow angle), the trimmed runs are glued on the plane instead: cuts that run within the two runs' tolerances of each other all along are sewn as one edge stating the gap, the others split where they cross, and the plane keeps a face where only one run's region covers it, looking out of that run; a solid that still fails the checks is refused by name rather than returned invalid; a round corner is refused where the law's next section is not the last turned about the corner, within what the runs are held to (a skinned run's tolerance), so a holed section's skinned run turns round ones too. The Frenet frame turns sharp corners extended or rounded the same way, each run's section set by the run's own Frenet frame, and is refused along a straight run, which has none. Round a smooth closed spine the auxiliary and binormal laws sweep as the rotation-minimizing frame where their frames are its frames turned by a fixed angle; otherwise their own frames, single-valued round the spine, are skinned round it, closed on themselves and held to the tolerance against the law, holes as void tunnels. Along an open spine those laws sweep a face with holes, each hole a solid of its own cut from the outer. Turned run by run, a closed wire sweeps the walls of the face it bounds, the end caps taken off. Round a closed spine of lines and arcs an open wire sweeps a ring of the exact sheet below, from the middle of the first leg round to there, where it closes on itself, each corner (the one where the spine closes too) mitred or rounded as down an open spine, and under a law as below; where the rotation-minimizing frame comes home turned (a spine out of one plane whose turns do not cancel) the ring would not close and is refused by name, as is a closed spine with any other edge. Down an open spine of lines and arcs under the rotation-minimizing frame an open wire sweeps one exact sheet: each line leg the prism of its section and each arc leg its revolution about the arc's axis, legs meeting tangent sewn on their common section, mitred on the plane halving each corner (an arc leg run on straight by the prism of its end section) or rounded (the section's part outside the turn turned about the corner). Inside a corner, mitred or rounded, each leg runs on until it meets the other's wall: on the halving plane between two lines, and where a corner against an arc turns in the arc's plane, on the conic a straight profile edge's two walls cross on, held exactly as a rational quadratic, or for a curved profile edge on a curve fitted through each of its points' exact crossings, its error stated as its tolerance; each profile edge is cut where it crosses the corner's axis and swept on its own, and both its walls are split on that one curve. The pieces are sewn and held to a disc whose boundary runs only along its end sections and the paths of the wire's ends; an extended corner, a leg shorter than its corners' reach (or a point's two paths meeting past a leg's end), a round turning too little to stand off its square end, a section reaching inside a corner that turns an arc out of its plane (its paths down the two legs pass each other without meeting) and a sheet that runs into itself are refused by name. The Frenet (rounded only), binormal and auxiliary laws sweep that sheet where their frames are the rotation-minimizing ones turned by a fixed angle, and are refused by name where they set a sharp corner's next section otherwise. Down an open spine with a leg that is neither a line nor an arc, or under a law whose frames are not those turned by a fixed angle along a spine with no sharp corner, an open wire sweeps one sheet of fitted skins held to the tolerance, uncapped: each profile edge a strip per run, neighbouring strips sharing their rails and neighbouring runs their rows. Its sharp corners follow the exact sheet's rules point by point: outside a mitred corner against a curved leg the end row runs on straight to the halving plane as two ruled faces sharing their exact cut, outside a round one it turns about the corner's axis, and inside either it runs on until its two paths cross; a point inside a corner whose paths pass each other, a turn too small to stand a round or run-on off its square end, and a law that sets a sharp corner's sections other than the rotation-minimizing frame turned by a fixed angle are refused by name.
